title: Fifth reason: every sin—even ‘venial’—offends infinite Majesty and deserves objectively and extensively infinite penalty
source_text: LXVIII. Denique omne peccatum, etiam illud quod veniale dicitur, infinitam Dei Majestatem offendit, ac proinde habet malitiam quodammodo, nimirum ob-jective, infinitam. Atque etiam macula ex quovis peccato contracta, ex se & seclusa Dei misericordia, in aeternum durat. Unde sequitur cuilibet peccato deberi poenam objective infinitam, quae nempe privet bono infinito; & praeterea, quae sit infinita extensive, id est, quae in aeternum duret, ut ita poena cum culpa proportionem habeat. Et sic peccatum quodvis natura sua mortale dici debet, utpote poena aeterna ex justitia plectendum.
pass_a_gloss: Finally every sin, even that which is called venial, offends the infinite Majesty of God, and therefore has a malice somehow infinite—namely objectively. And also the stain contracted from any sin, of itself and with God’s mercy shut out, lasts forever. Whence it follows that to any sin there is due a penalty objectively infinite, which namely deprives of an infinite good; and besides, which is infinite extensively—that is, which lasts forever—so that thus the penalty may have proportion with the guilt. And so any sin ought to be called mortal by its nature, as to be punished with eternal penalty from justice.
pass_b_english: Closing proof: even so-called venial sin strikes infinite Majesty—objective infinite malice—and leaves an unending stain apart from mercy.
Due penalty is infinite in object and in everlasting extent; therefore every sin is mortal by nature under justice.
